**Paddle:** Solid face, short handle — basically an oversized table-tennis racket. No strings.

Yes — repurposing is streamlining when the barrier is **infrastructure**, not rules or time. You don't build a new venue; you play on what's already there.

**Sports examples:**

| What exists | What gets repurposed | Why it works |
|-------------|---------------------|--------------|
| Badminton court (20' × 44') | **Pickleball** | Same footprint, lower net — invented on one in 1965 |
| Tennis court pad | **Four pickleball courts** | Spread without new construction |
| Basketball gym floor | **Futsal** / indoor soccer | Every school already has the room |
| Half a basketball hoop | **3x3** | Six players, one end of an existing court |
| Any flat patch + tennis ball | **Street cricket** | No pitch required |
| Tennis court footprint | **Padel** cage | Court within a court |

**Board-game version:** same idea, but the "infrastructure" is your table. Card games in a travel pouch, **Catan: On the Road**, city **Ticket to Ride** maps — games sized for a desk or hotel counter, not a dedicated game table.

It's distinct from "shrink the space" (design a smaller court) and "invent the cousin" (build a new sport). Repurposing says: *the streamlined version fits hardware someone already paid for.*

I added a **Repurpose what's already built** section and a row in the summary table.
